name: Eye color change drops

lead: Eye color change drops refers to the idea, discussed on looksmaxxing forums, that a topical product can lighten the iris. No published human study has tested an over-the-counter or homemade drop for this purpose. The better-documented drug effect runs the other way: the glaucoma medicine latanoprost can increase iris pigment in some people.

In practice the forum conversation is mostly about procedures rather than drops: corneal tattooing (keratopigmentation), laser iris depigmentation and cosmetic iris implants. Review articles describe these as having limited long-term data and, for implants, serious complications.

paras: Iris color depends largely on the amount of melanin in the iris stroma. Prostaglandin-analogue drops such as latanoprost are reported to raise the melanin content of stromal melanocytes, which darkens the eye. Surgical methods work differently: keratopigmentation places pigment in the cornea, laser depigmentation uses a Nd:YAG laser to remove stromal melanin, and implants cover the iris with a colored artificial disc.

Reviews report that cosmetic iris implants are not approved by major regulators and have been linked to glaucoma, uveitis, corneal damage and vision loss. Laser depigmentation has limited long-term safety data, and keratopigmentation is described as the most studied option but still lacking long-term cosmetic evidence. Unregulated drops placed in the eye carry the general risk of contamination and infection, a point raised by forum posters themselves.

lead: Eye color change drops is a term used in looksmaxxing communities for eye drops that are claimed to lighten the color of the iris, usually from brown toward blue, green or hazel. No peer-reviewed study has examined a cosmetic drop for lightening eye color. [1]

The prescription drug most often connected to the topic is latanoprost, a glaucoma medicine whose labelled side effects include increased brown iris pigmentation, meaning it tends to darken rather than lighten eyes. Microscopy studies attribute the change to more melanin inside existing iris melanocytes. [2][3]

Forum discussion largely moves from drops to procedures. Published reviews describe three surgical approaches to cosmetic eye color change: iris implants, laser iris depigmentation and cosmetic keratopigmentation, with the evidence base strongest for the last and weakest for implants' safety. [1][4][5]
infobox: Topical drops; corneal tattoo; laser; implant
Drug linked to iris color change
Cosmetic iris implants are not FDA-approved or CE-marked [1]

paras: The phrase covers several separate things that forum users sometimes conflate: over-the-counter or homemade drops said to lighten the iris, prescription drops that incidentally change iris color, and clinic procedures that change apparent eye color. On looksmax.org, one detailed post by a user who reports having had laser depigmentation says they do not believe in drops, and warns that preparing eye drops without medical training carries a high infection rate. [6]

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue used for glaucoma and ocular hypertension; it is prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia and the EU and was approved in 1996. Increased brown iris pigmentation is listed among its common effects. [7]

A review of iris histology after latanoprost concluded that the darkening is likely due to more melanin within iris stromal melanocytes rather than more melanocytes, and that susceptible individuals, particularly those with hazel eyes, are most affected. The authors noted that numbers of specimens examined were small. [2] A 3-month randomized study of 17 glaucoma patients found no degenerative or proliferative iris changes, with one case of color change among the treated eyes. [8] An earlier case report examined an iridectomy specimen from a patient with latanoprost-induced color change. [3]
Forum threads ask whether latanoprost or the related eyelash product Latisse can change eye color. [9][10] The published drug literature describes darkening, not lightening.

Keratopigmentation, or corneal tattooing, has a history reaching back to antiquity and was developed in modern form in the 19th century; Francis Ferrari is credited with first using it for cosmetic purposes on healthy eyes, and femtosecond-laser versions are sometimes called FLAAK. Reported risks include fading pigment, corneal erosions, keratitis and ulceration. [11]

A 2025 narrative review describes three main surgical approaches: cosmetic iris implants, laser iris depigmentation and keratopigmentation. It says implants, repurposed from treatment of iris defects, carry severe risks including glaucoma, endothelial cell loss and permanent vision impairment and are widely considered unsafe; laser depigmentation gives a natural look but has potential complications such as patchy pigmentation, photophobia and temporary pressure spikes, with limited long-term data; and keratopigmentation was reported as the safest of the three. [1]

A 2022 review described cosmetic iris implants as lacking CE marking and FDA approval and associated with uveitis, hyphema, glaucoma, cataract and vision loss, and noted that scientific data on laser depigmentation are very limited. [4] A 2026 review in Cornea reported generally favorable short-term outcomes and high patient satisfaction in selected cases but called for long-term evidence, pigment standardization and careful patient selection. [5]

No studies found on drops sold or made to lighten eye color. Related research covers latanoprost-induced iris darkening in glaucoma patients [2][8] and surgical cosmetic eye-color procedures, which are described mainly in case series and reviews rather than controlled trials. [1][4][5]

Posters on looksmax.org describe lighter eyes as a desirable feature and discuss saving money for clinic procedures abroad, with other posters disputing the quality of particular clinics' results. [9][12] One thread author says some people had reported fake before-and-after images from clinics, and that implant feedback shared online can be dangerous. [6] Another thread quotes a clinic's marketing that it carries no side effects or risks, a statement that differs from the complication profile in published reviews. [12][1]

lore.intro: Eye color is discussed on looksmax.org as a feature that can be changed, with debate about which method is safe and whether the results look natural. [9][6]
